incidents.name: b14g
incidents.description: On October 31, 2026, an attacker withdrew approximately 97 million CORE from assets staked through b14g and transferred them to attacker-controlled addresses. The protocol paused the affected contracts and coordinated with security partners and exchanges to trace the stolen funds. Approximately 68 million CORE remained on Core, while exchanges froze another 9 million CORE. BTC staked through b14g was unaffected and remained time-locked on Bitcoin

incidents.name: Troves
incidents.description: On October 31, an attacker exploited permissions retained by a legacy rebalancing contract after it had been replaced, resulting in approximately 8.6 BTC in losses from Troves' xWBTC/WBTC vault. Troves revoked the legacy contract's permissions and paused three vaults as a precaution. No impact on other vaults has been identified

incidents.name: Polymarket International
incidents.description: Attackers reportedly compromised a third-party website monitoring service used by Polymarket, allowing malicious JavaScript to execute on its international trading platform. The script hijacked authenticated trading sessions to sell prediction-market positions and transfer assets to attacker-controlled wallets. Polymarket temporarily suspended trading, removed the affected integration, and committed to reimbursing impacted users

incidents.name: Binance CEX
incidents.description: On October 29, attackers exploited Binance’s operational infrastructure to execute unauthorized withdrawals across multiple blockchains, resulting in approximately $6.3 billion in losses. Binance’s preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that allowed access to a service container, with no evidence of wallet private key leakage. Approximately $3 billion in stolen assets were later frozen with help from industry partners. Binance committed to covering all losses using its SAFU fund and company reserves

incidents.name: zkLink Nova
incidents.description: An attacker exploited zkLink’s Arbitrator contract, which failed to clear a previously authenticated message hash after processing a claim. By reusing that hash through the publicly accessible SyncL2TxHashRelayer, the attacker impersonated an authorized gateway message and installed a malicious L2 logs root. The attacker then submitted forged withdrawal proofs against the compromised root to drain approximately $783,100 from zkLink’s Ethereum bridge

incidents.name: Hifi Finance
incidents.description: An attacker acquired HIFI governance tokens and used four coordinated votes shortly before voting closed to pass a malicious governance proposal. Proposal 21 would upgrade Hifi’s BalanceSheet contract to introduce a function that incorrectly treats existing collateral as untracked funds, allowing it to be transferred to an attacker-controlled Safe. The proposal would also mint 25 million HIFI tokens to the attacker. At the time of reporting, the proposal was queued but had not been executed

incidents.name: Fence Finance
incidents.description: An attacker exploited a tranche vault associated with Fence Finance and Valinor Digital by using a flash loan to obtain an inflated allocation of vault shares. The attacker subsequently redeemed those shares to withdraw approximately $1.01 million in USDC from the vault

incidents.name: Zilliqa X-Bridge
incidents.description: Zilliqa confirmed a security incident affecting its X-Bridge and ZRC2 proxy contracts associated with certain liquidity pools, including PlunderSwap. The affected assets include zUSDT, SEED, kUSD, and Zoge, while native ZIL and the Zilliqa EVM network reportedly remain unaffected. X-Bridge remains paused while operational keys are rotated and investigations continue

incidents.name: Predict Fun
incidents.description: Several Predict.fun users experienced unauthorized wallet transfers totaling approximately 400,000 USDT. Preliminary findings suggest a possible compromise of the project’s API documentation website, which was hosted by a third-party provider. Predict.fun took the documentation site offline as a precaution and committed to reimbursing affected users

incidents.name: Bloom Trading Bot
incidents.description: An attacker exploited a reported remote code execution vulnerability in a third-party software module used by Bloom’s trading infrastructure, enabling unauthorized transfers from user wallets. Approximately 9,408 SOL was drained from 48 wallets belonging to nine traders within 94 seconds. Bloom attributed the incident to the third-party module and denied that private keys were exposed, while Bitquery confirmed that the transactions were signed using the affected wallets’ keys

incidents.name: Myriad Markets
incidents.description: An attacker exploited a previously exposed private key belonging to Myriad’s automated market management wallet. The key had reportedly been leaked through a vulnerability in a third-party library used by a backend service. The attacker used the wallet’s privileges to manipulate positions and force incorrect resolutions across 10 prediction markets on BNB Chain. Myriad revoked the wallet’s permissions, secured the remaining funds, and announced that all affected markets would be voided and users refunded

incidents.name: Yapeswap
incidents.description: YapeSwap’s WorkersUnion governance contract allowed proposals to pass with zero quorum, enabling an attacker controlling approximately 0.000055% of voting power to transfer YapeFactory’s feeToSetter role to themselves. The attacker then installed a malicious Registry that returned fake vault addresses through latestVault(), while vaults() continued listing legitimate vaults. This redirected deposits into attacker-controlled destinations while YapePair incorrectly accounted for them as farming assets, resulting in approximately $21,900 in losses

incidents.name: X100
incidents.description: X100’s governance system allowed an attacker to obtain two of three Senate seats using flash-loan-funded X tokens. The attacker immediately used this majority to approve and execute a malicious treasury proposal within the same transaction. The proposal forced the Freezer to swap 400,000 X tokens into an attacker-controlled liquidity pool with zero minimum output, allowing the attacker to extract treasury value through a manipulated trade

incidents.name: Initia
incidents.description: Initia suffered a security incident involving the unauthorized minting of multiple assets on its L1. The attacker reportedly transferred and converted some of the minted assets into Ethereum-based holdings. Initia halted its L1 and rollups while investigating the vulnerability and coordinating with validators, exchanges, and security teams

incidents.name: WAX Multi-Chain Bridge
incidents.description: WAX’s eth.token::withdraw function failed to validate that max_fee was nonnegative. By setting max_fee = -quantity, the attacker reduced the total account debit to zero while retaining the full withdrawal amount. Because the configured withdrawal fee was zero, the fee check did not reject the transaction. The resulting withdrawal logs triggered real payouts from the bridge on Solana and Ethereum

incidents.name: Swell
incidents.description: An attacker gained control of approximately 30 Swell operational keys across multiple networks, including the swETH/rswETH oracle bot. The attacker drained wallet balances, artificially increased swETH and rswETH exchange rates by submitting unbacked reserve values, and redirected EigenLayer reward claims. They also deployed malicious upgrade contracts capable of draining approximately 2,513 ETH, although these upgrades had not been approved or executed when the investigation was published

incidents.name: CoinDCX
incidents.description: CoinDCX experienced approximately $16 million in suspicious outflows from TRON addresses associated with its exchange infrastructure. The exchange attributed the incident to addresses compromised during its July 2025 security breach, which continued receiving deposits after being deprecated. CoinDCX acknowledged that its deposit-sweeping process failed temporarily and stated that it absorbed the resulting losses while crediting affected users. Investigators disputed whether the addresses had genuinely been removed from active operations

incidents.name: Vara Bridge
incidents.description: An attacker reportedly exploited Vara Bridge's cross-chain proof verification process to submit fraudulent Merkle roots representing outbound messages from Vara. These roots allegedly enabled unauthorized messages to be processed on Ethereum, resulting in approximately $12,776 in losses

incidents.name: AlpsCon AI Trade Hub
incidents.description: AlpsCon AI Trade Hub’s V7–V9 contracts incorrectly applied accumulated historical profit-per-share values to balances imported from preceding versions, allowing newly deposited funds to claim rewards accrued before the deposits existed. The attacker used a flash loan to create temporary ALPS service credits and exploited the accounting flaw to extract USDC. The attack was facilitated by an authorization whitelist containing a publicly known Hardhat test account, which the attacker used through EIP-7702 delegation

incidents.name: Coffer
incidents.description: Coffer’s BTC pool incorrectly rounded tiny deposits to zero while still minting LP tokens, allowing an attacker to repeatedly obtain shares without providing equivalent assets. The attacker submitted thousands of minimal deposits, diluting existing liquidity providers and minting approximately $18 in illegitimate LP tokens. Coffer paused its pools on October 18, preventing further withdrawals, and deployed a fix on October 19

incidents.name: Qubic
incidents.description: An attacker exploited predictable wallet seeds generated with insufficient randomness in Qubic’s wallet software, compromising 1,404 user wallets and stealing approximately 2.94 trillion QU. The vulnerability affected certain wallets created on Apple devices and Safari browsers. Qubic halted its network at tick 85,371,949, while MEXC froze the account receiving the remaining stolen funds. Seed generation was corrected in wallet version 4.26.4

incidents.name: Pirate Chain
incidents.description: Pirate Chain suffered an exploit in the transparent supply-accounting layer introduced with its Ironwood upgrade. Two transaction-validation failures reportedly allowed an attacker to bypass issuance restrictions and exploit incorrect output-script interpretation, creating approximately 39.8 million unauthorized ARRR. The tokens were transferred into the Sapling shielded pool, obscuring subsequent transfers. The team initially proposed a blockchain rollback but later confirmed that it could not execute one unilaterally

incidents.name: Affluent
incidents.description: Affluent’s lending vaults reportedly suffered unauthorized share minting that allowed attackers to redeem vault assets without providing corresponding deposits. The supplied analysis identifies suspicious transactions on September 30, October 12, and October 16, 2026, involving multiple wallets. Extracted assets were reportedly transferred through exchanges, swaps, and cross-chain services

incidents.name: UNCX Network V2
incidents.description: An attacker exploited UNCX Vesting V2’s shared token accounting by creating vesting positions, releasing a large position, donating tokens into the pool, and cancelling a topped-up vest. This sequence allowed a small remaining vesting position to withdraw tokens belonging to other users. UNCX confirmed additional affected assets across four chains and introduced emergency fees and restrictions to contain the exploit

incidents.name: Gamdom
incidents.description: Gamdom suffered a multichain hot-wallet compromise following unauthorized access to an automation server. Investigators traced approximately $4.21M in stolen assets across eight networks. The attacker subsequently bridged, swapped, and distributed funds through multiple wallets and services, including Mayan, Hyperliquid, and THORChain. The precise mechanism used to obtain control of the wallets remains unconfirmed

incidents.name: Papertrade
incidents.description: Papertrade, a perpetual trading protocol on HyperEVM, reportedly suffered an oracle manipulation attack shortly after launch. The attacker manipulated Hyperliquid’s ETH order-book midpoint through external trades while opening and closing highly leveraged synthetic positions on Papertrade. Because the protocol used the instantaneous BBO midpoint without TWAP, deviation limits, or independent price validation, manipulated prices were accepted for execution and PnL settlement, transferring approximately $1.28M from the Martingaler LP

incidents.name: Ledger (Supply Chain)
incidents.description: Attackers purchased genuine Ledger hardware wallets, installed concealed components capable of capturing recovery phrases, and redistributed the modified devices through resellers. The implants monitored the wallets’ displays during initialization and transmitted captured recovery phrases through cellular connections. Attackers subsequently derived users’ private keys and drained their cryptocurrency holdings. Ledger confirmed that its Secure Element, operating system, and internal infrastructure were not compromised

incidents.name: BitBay
incidents.description: BitBay’s vault contained a vulnerability in _withdraw() that transferred the contract’s entire token balance whenever liquidity == 0, without restricting withdrawals to the user’s proportional entitlement. The attacker triggered this condition through reposition() and subsequently redeemed one minimal share unit, receiving approximately 14,838.47 DAI belonging to the vault

incidents.name: Ethervista
incidents.description: EtherVista’s EtherVistaPair.swap() contained an integer overflow vulnerability in its constant-product invariant check. Because the contract multiplied two uint112 reserves without sufficient overflow protection, the calculation could wrap around and incorrectly validate swaps that reduced the pool’s actual reserve product. An attacker registered a malicious contract as an authorized router and executed two crafted swaps to withdraw WETH and VISTA from the pool

incidents.name: Set Protocol
incidents.description: ETHMACOAPY’s actualizeFee() rounded redemption backing upward even when no fee was payable. Attackers donated collateral to trigger recalculation, temporarily acquired Set tokens, then redeemed them for more collateral than they contributed, with the difference coming from existing holders’ backing. Two separate EOAs repeated the process across two transactions, draining approximately 8.11 WETH

incidents.name: MakerDAO ETH-A Liquidation Keeper Bot
incidents.description: A dormant third-party MakerDAO ETH-A liquidation keeper had an unprotected drain routine that lacked ds-auth authorization. Any caller could invoke the function and provide the withdrawal recipient. The attacker triggered Flipper.deal() for four auctions the keeper had won in 2020, causing 200 WETH of previously unclaimed collateral to move through Vat.flux to the keeper, then used GemJoin.exit() to send it to an attacker-controlled recipient and unwrap it to ETH. MakerDAO’s core contracts behaved as designed; the vulnerability was in the third-party keeper

incidents.name: GoldPesa
incidents.description: GoldPesa’s GPXHooks rebalanced protocol-owned GPX/USDC liquidity through Uniswap v4’s shared PositionManager without ensuring its currency deltas were isolated and settled. An attacker created an unpaid WETH/USDC position within the same PoolManager unlock and then triggered GoldPesa’s hourly rebalance. Because TAKE_PAIR operated on the PositionManager’s net credit, GoldPesa’s legitimate USDC credit offset the attacker’s outstanding debt, allowing the attacker to burn their position and withdraw the resulting USDC. Uniswap v4 itself behaved as designed

incidents.name: FlashLoopAdapter
incidents.description: FlashLoopAdapter’s open()/close() authorization trusted any caller whose isModuleEnabled() response returned true, allowing an attacker-controlled fake Safe to pass the check. The attacker then supplied each real victim Safe as swapRouter and encoded execTransactionFromModule(...) as arbitrary swapCalldata. Because FlashLoopAdapter was already an enabled module on those Safes, they accepted the calls and transferred or withdrew collateral to the attacker

incidents.name: NEAR Intents
incidents.description: NEAR Intents was exploited through a bug in the interaction between its Omni deposit and withdrawal infrastructure and the NEAR Intents smart contract, allowing unauthorized withdrawals. The team stopped services, patched the contract-side vulnerability, and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals across multiple networks while completing fixes to the Omni infrastructure. The stolen funds were traced toward KuCoin and then BTC, and NEAR Intents said the losses would be compensated in full

incidents.name: SKYDAO
incidents.description: SKYDAO’s taxed sell flow called its pool controller before the seller’s net tokens were credited to the PancakeSwap V2 pair. The controller sold the 35% tax, moved the gross sell amount from the pair to the dead address through controlburn(), and called pair.sync(), causing the pair to record an almost-zero SKYDAO reserve. When the original transfer subsequently credited the net SKYDAO to the pair without updating that recorded reserve, the attacker exploited the balance/reserve mismatch through pair.swap() to extract USDT liquidity

incidents.name: Fake GIWA Bridge
incidents.description: Scammers deployed a counterfeit OP Stack-style network impersonating GIWA, including an RPC endpoint, Ethereum bridge and batch-posting infrastructure. The fake network reported GIWA’s expected mainnet Chain ID 9134, causing DYORSWAP and users to mistake it for the legitimate GIWA mainnet. Users voluntarily deposited ETH into the fraudulent bridge. After accumulating deposits, the scammers drained 766.25 ETH to an attacker-controlled address. GIWA’s actual mainnet had not launched, and neither GIWA nor DYORSWAP’s smart contracts were exploited

incidents.name: Demex Perp
incidents.description: Demex’s bridge was exploited through insufficient verification between its bridge module and external-chain contract system. The attacker used a helper contract to falsify token-deployment reports, registering the low-value nLEND token against canonical WETH and WBNB contracts. Subsequent withdrawals released approximately $191,929 in bridge reserves despite deducting only $10.47 worth of nLEND. The withdrawal limiter also failed because it valued the deducted tokens rather than the assets released

incidents.name: Duelbits
incidents.description: Duelbits suffered unauthorized transfers from hot wallets across Ethereum, BSC, Bitcoin, and Tron. Stolen assets were rapidly moved, bridged and largely consolidated into ETH and DAI on Ethereum. Duelbits took its platform offline while investigating and stated that user funds were safe. Security researchers suspect compromise of hot-wallet private keys, but Duelbits has not yet published a technical root cause

incidents.name: Bitget
incidents.description: Bitget detected unauthorized transfers involving a limited number of hot wallets at 18:31 UTC on September 24. Subsequent tracing identified approximately $387.5M transferred to attacker-controlled addresses across Ethereum and other EVM networks, XRP Ledger, Zcash and Tron. Bitget states that the incident has been contained and no further unauthorized transfers are possible
incidents.actor: North Korea (per Chainalysis, referenced in Binance analysis)
